claims.text: Tailored thermal treatments can effectively direct phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Combining controlled cooling rates with an intermediate isothermal annealing step promotes nucleation and growth of ordered secondary phases.
The initial as-cast or rapidly cooled Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA is a metastable, mostly disordered solid solution.
A defined cooling rate followed by an isothermal hold at a target temperature under an inert atmosphere can control phase evolution.
The treatment forms ordered secondary phases, including nanoscale precipitates, within the disordered matrix.
Controlled thermal energy input modulates atomic diffusion.
Modulation of atomic diffusion adjusts phase-transformation kinetics.
Adjusted phase-transformation kinetics lead to nucleation and growth of thermodynamically favored ordered phases.
The ordered phases alter the mechanical properties of the alloy.
The thermal treatment produces more distinct and stable secondary phases than occur in the untreated or as-quenched state.
The treatment-induced secondary phases are observable using XRD and microscopy.
The thermal treatment increases hardness relative to the untreated or as-quenched state.
The method is applicable across the established compositional range of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The effectiveness of the method depends on precise tuning of cooling and annealing parameters.
Overly aggressive thermal treatments can cause undesirable microstructural coarsening.
